title: Reading slowly
hookLine: reading for information and reading for formation are different speeds

lines: A LETTER FOUND IN A DRAWER.
cards: The terms and conditions on a new app: scroll, scroll, agree. Now a different page: a letter in a drawer, in the handwriting of someone who has died, found years later. That one gets read slowly.
A pause at a phrase. A second reading. One sentence, ten times over, until the voice comes back.
Same eyes, same alphabet, completely different reading. Headlines, feeds and emails tend to get the first speed: skimming for what's needed.
Some Christian teachers say the Bible is meant to be read, at least sometimes, at the second.

teach.b: Some Christian writers call the two speeds reading for information and reading for formation. The first asks: what does this say? The second asks: what is this doing to me?
Both matter, they say: the first tells you what's there, and the second is where the words start to shape a life. The Bible itself describes the slow kind.
The first psalm, the one from three days ago, praises the person whose "delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night."
That word meditate, in Hebrew hagah, doesn't mean sitting silent with an empty mind. It means to murmur, to mutter under your breath. Isaiah uses the same word for a lion growling over its prey.

teach.h: A LION THAT WON'T LET GO.
teach.b: So the picture is someone going over the words out loud, again and again, low and slow, like a lion that won't let go.
Augustine, in his Confessions, describes watching the bishop Ambrose read with his eyes moving and his voice silent, and wondering why.
Some medieval monks called slow reading rumination: chewing on the words the way a cow chews the cud. You met their method on day one hundred one, lectio divina: read, notice a word, ponder, rest.
Christians from different churches read this way in some form: monks and nuns, some Protestants with a single verse in a morning quiet time, people who imagine themselves into a Gospel scene.
At full speed, the words pass through you.
Slowed down, one word can hold you for a whole minute.

how: Some Christians read scripture slowly, often aloud or under their breath, repeating a phrase and pausing on a word; monks and nuns practice this as lectio divina, and some Protestants read a single verse slowly in a morning quiet time.

o: reading for formation, letting the words shape you
reading with trouble, struggling over each word
reading in silence, without moving your lips

games.q: what's inside slow reading — tap the pairs.

s: in Psalm 1, meditate means emptying your mind
hagah means to murmur, going over the words again and again.
Augustine was surprised to see a bishop reading silently
he describes it in his Confessions and wonders why the bishop read that way.
reading slowly means you can't also read for information
both speeds matter. one tells you what's there; the other lets it shape you.

games.q: you're a medieval monk with one page of scripture and an hour. how do you read it?
o: as fast as you can, then move on.
you don't; you just look at the pictures.
games.why: monks called it rumination: murmuring the words and going over them again and again, like chewing the cud.

practice: If you have a Bible, open to Psalm 23 and take the first five verses; if not, its first line: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want."

Read it once at normal speed, then again twice as slowly, murmuring under your breath, and when one word catches you, stop there and say it again. If you pray, let that word become your prayer; if you don't, just stay with it.

wordCard.voice: Reading slowly. Reading for formation, not only information: murmuring the words until one stops you. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: to murmur, to mutter. the word for meditate in Psalm 1:2.

carryVoice: Your line: slow down to hear. Information first, then formation. That's one hundred twenty-nine days.
